hub.title: The Eucharistic Miracles of the World
hub.eyebrow: In the footsteps of Saint Carlo Acutis
hub.intro: From Lanciano to Faverney, explore source-grounded accounts of Eucharistic devotion, one place at a time. This is a growing independent collection inspired by Saint Carlo’s exhibition, not an official reproduction or a complete catalogue.
hub.carloText: Saint Carlo Acutis helped create an international exhibition of Eucharistic miracles. This independent collection continues his invitation to pay attention to the Eucharist, with original writing and direct links to the sanctuaries, dioceses and historical records behind each account. Carlo was canonized on September 7, 2025.
hub.methodText: A tradition is a tradition. A diocesan investigation is not the same as a universal declaration. Scientific observations do not establish a supernatural cause. Each page names its source and distinguishes what was reported from what can be independently concluded. This growing collection is not every reported miracle in the world.
hub.note: Independent devotional collection. Not affiliated with the Carlo Acutis Association.
hub.charbelEntryIntro: Explore ten source-grounded Eucharistic accounts from Italy, Portugal, Poland, Croatia, the Netherlands, Spain and France in an original, independent collection inspired by Saint Carlo’s exhibition. Each page distinguishes tradition from documented inquiry.

lanciano.title: Lanciano: A Witness Kept in Abruzzo
lanciano.label: The ancient witness
lanciano.alt: The reliquary kept in the sanctuary at Lanciano
lanciano.sourceLabel: Sanctuary of the Eucharistic Miracle of Lanciano
lanciano.lead: An ancient account of doubt at Mass, and a presence still venerated in a Franciscan sanctuary.
sections: The story as the sanctuary tells it

A monk of the Eastern rite was celebrating Mass in Lanciano when he struggled with belief in the Real Presence. According to the sanctuary tradition, the bread and wine visibly changed. The monk is unnamed. The sanctuary places the account broadly in the eighth century, perhaps between 730 and 750; it says no source fixes an exact day or year.
The witness today

The relics remain at the Church of San Francesco. The sanctuary traces their preservation through successive communities and describes examinations over the centuries. A written account dating to 1631 is much later than the event it describes, a distinction worth keeping in view.
What examination can say

The sanctuary reports laboratory examination of samples in 1970-71, including findings described as human cardiac tissue and blood group AB. Those are its account of a particular examination; a laboratory result cannot by itself establish the ancient event, divine causation, or a complete chain of custody across twelve centuries.
lanciano.reflection: In the story, doubt is not the end of prayer. Bring difficult questions into the quiet of the Mass without demanding that a sign replace faith.

bolsena-orvieto.title: Bolsena and Orvieto: The Corporal
bolsena-orvieto.label: The linen and the feast
bolsena-orvieto.alt: The reliquary of the Corporal at Orvieto
bolsena-orvieto.sourceLabel: Opera del Duomo di Orvieto, Chapel of the Corporal
bolsena-orvieto.lead: A linen cloth carried from Bolsena to Orvieto became the center of a chapel and a lasting procession.
sections: A priest on the road

The cathedral of Orvieto recounts that a Bohemian priest celebrating Mass in Bolsena saw drops of blood stain the altar linen. He was traveling toward Rome. The account names Peter of Prague but presents the details as tradition; the chapel now houses the corporal.
From Bolsena to Orvieto

The cathedral relates that Pope Urban IV had the linen brought to Orvieto and established the feast of Corpus Christi. Orvieto still honors the corporal in an annual procession. This story belongs to the city and its liturgical memory, not merely to an image of the relic.
A date handled carefully

The cathedral places the event in 1263 and associates the feast with the papal bull of 1264. Carlo Acutis’s exhibition catalogue lists Bolsena under 1264. We follow the cathedral’s chronology here and show the disagreement rather than quietly picking one date.
bolsena-orvieto.reflection: A small cloth has carried a long public memory. What helps you notice the quiet holiness of an ordinary Mass?

siena.title: Siena: The Hosts Kept Across Centuries
siena.label: A recovered treasure
siena.alt: Exterior of the Basilica of San Francesco in Siena, where the hosts are kept
siena.sourceLabel: Archdiocese of Siena, history of the Eucharistic event
siena.lead: A theft, a recovery, and hosts long guarded by the people of Siena.
sections: August 1730

According to the Archdiocese of Siena, thieves took a ciborium containing 351 consecrated hosts from the Basilica of San Francesco on August 14. The hosts were found on August 17 in the nearby sanctuary of Santa Maria in Provenzano and returned to San Francesco in procession.
What is preserved

In its 2014 account, the archdiocese said 223 hosts remained and are venerated in the basilica. It describes repeated examinations and quotes a 1914 commission on their unusual preservation. The numbers, tests and devotional interpretation are those reported by the archdiocese, not an independent modern verification by this site.
More than an anomaly

In Siena the story also carries a memory of loss and recovery: people sought what had been taken and kept watch over what came back. The archdiocese records the continuing devotion around the hosts and the annual remembrance of their discovery.
siena.reflection: To guard something sacred is also to give it attention. Consider one small act of reverence you can offer this week.

santarem.title: Santarém: A Light in the Story
santarem.label: A Portuguese devotion
santarem.alt: Church of Saint Stephen, the Sanctuary of the Most Holy Miracle in Santarém
santarem.sourceLabel: Diocese of Santarém, Sanctuary of the Most Holy Miracle
santarem.lead: A story of a hidden host, a reported light, and a sanctuary still visited today.
sections: A complicated human story

The Diocese of Santarém recounts a woman in a painful marriage who removed a consecrated host from church after seeking help from a sorceress. In the tradition, the cloth holding the host began to bleed. Later, she and her husband saw light from the chest where she had put it. They told the parish priest, and the host was brought back to the church.
A sanctuary in the city

The Church of Saint Stephen is now the Sanctuary of the Most Holy Miracle. The diocese describes centuries of local processions and devotion associated with the host. The story must not be used to excuse abuse in the woman’s marriage; her suffering deserves compassion, not blame.
When did it happen?
The diocese gives 1266, or 1247 according to some chroniclers. That difference is part of the historical record. This page does not claim that either year is settled.
santarem.reflection: What was hidden in the story came into a community’s care. Pray for those carrying fear or harm in silence, and offer them real help where you can.

sokolka.title: Sokółka: A Commission’s Careful Account
sokolka.label: A modern inquiry
sokolka.alt: Exterior of Saint Anthony of Padua church in Sokółka, Poland
sokolka.sourceLabel: Białystok Metropolitan Curia, commission statement, October 14, 2009
sokolka.lead: In Poland, a diocesan commission recorded what it examined, and what it did not claim to prove.
sections: What happened in church

The Białystok Metropolitan Curia says that on October 12, 2008, a consecrated host fell during Communion. It was placed in water. On October 19, staff saw a red mark on it. The curia set up a commission in March 2009 to review witnesses and specialists’ findings.
A measured finding

The curia reports that two independent pathomorphologists found the sample resembled heart muscle tissue more than other living tissues. Their wording says “indicates” or “most resembles,” not that they established a supernatural cause. The commission said it found no outside interference and forwarded its records to the Apostolic Nunciature.
What the statement concludes

The curia concluded that the event did not contradict the Church’s faith and called for reverence toward the Eucharist. This site does not upgrade that statement into a claim of Vatican certification or independent scientific proof of a miracle.
sokolka.reflection: The commission’s care is part of this story. Reverence need not make us less truthful; it can make us more attentive to what is known and what remains a mystery.

legnica.title: Legnica: A Bishop’s Public Account
legnica.label: A diocesan inquiry
legnica.alt: Saint Hyacinth Church in Legnica, where the host is displayed
legnica.sourceLabel: Bishop of Legnica, communiqué published by the Sanctuary of St. Hyacinth
legnica.lead: A fallen host, a diocesan inquiry, and public veneration authorized after consultation with Rome.
sections: The account begins at Communion

Bishop Zbigniew Kiernikowski’s communiqué dates the event to Christmas Day 2013 at Saint Hyacinth’s church. A consecrated host fell during Communion and was placed in water. A red discoloration later appeared. His predecessor set up a commission to observe the phenomenon; in February 2014 a fragment of the red material was placed on a corporal for examination.
What the investigators reported

The bishop quoted a forensic assessment describing fragments of striated muscle whose overall appearance was most similar to heart muscle, and said genetic tests indicated human origin. These are findings reported in a diocesan communiqué; they cannot alone establish how the material got there or a supernatural cause. This site has not independently inspected the samples or the full laboratory records.
A decision about veneration

Kiernikowski said he submitted the case to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in January and, following recommendations of the Holy See, directed the parish to prepare a place for the relic and teach visitors about Eucharistic devotion. The Diocese of Legnica reports that the relic was offered for public veneration on July 2, 2016, with the Holy See’s agreement. The bishop described an event with the hallmarks of a Eucharistic miracle; permission for veneration is not the same as a Vatican declaration of supernatural origin.
legnica.reflection: The bishop asked for prayer and careful teaching rather than a laboratory result standing alone. What would it mean to bring both reverence and honest questions to the Eucharist?

ludbreg.title: Ludbreg: The Chalice and a Public Devotion
ludbreg.label: An early papal permission
ludbreg.alt: Sanctuary of the Most Precious Blood of Christ in Ludbreg, Croatia
ludbreg.sourceLabel: Archdiocese of Zagreb, account of the Ludbreg devotion
ludbreg.source2Label: Holy See Press Office, papal envoy for the 600th anniversary
ludbreg.lead: A fifteenth-century account of blood in a chalice, followed by inquiry and permission for public veneration.
sections: A priest and a chalice

The Archdiocese of Zagreb recounts a Mass in Ludbreg in 1411. In the local account, a priest doubted the Real Presence and then saw what seemed to be fresh blood in the chalice. He put the chalice aside and finished Mass. This is a historical devotional tradition, told in a later archdiocesan account; the priest’s observation is not a laboratory finding or a contemporaneous record reproduced here.
A reported inquiry in Rome

The archdiocesan account says Pope Julius II sent representatives to investigate, hear witnesses and examine reports of healings associated with the relic. It names the papal representative and local participants. The archdiocese reports that Julius died before finishing the matter, and that his successor Leo X permitted public veneration of the relic in 1513. Its account dates the bull to March 12; a regional tourism source gives April 14. Because those dates conflict, this page uses the year without claiming a settled day.
A devotion that continues

The sanctuary in Ludbreg remains a place of pilgrimage. In 2011, the Holy See named a papal envoy to the close of the 600th-anniversary celebrations. That recognition of a pilgrimage and its history is not a modern scientific finding about the substance in the chalice. The Church’s permission for public veneration belongs to the story; it should not be recast as a new Vatican certification of every detail of the event.
ludbreg.reflection: The account begins with doubt and ends with a community keeping watch across generations. What can patient attention teach us at Mass, even when history leaves questions open?

amsterdam.title: Amsterdam: A Host and a Silent Walk
amsterdam.label: A city’s long memory
amsterdam.alt: Interior of the Begijnhof Catholic Chapel in Amsterdam, where devotion to the Miracle continued
amsterdam.sourceLabel: Society of the Silent Walk, account of the Amsterdam tradition
amsterdam.source2Label: Bishop of Haarlem-Amsterdam, 2025 lecture on the miracle and Eucharistic devotion
amsterdam.lead: A medieval account of a host surviving fire became a city procession, then a quiet nighttime walk.
sections: The story on Kalverstraat

According to the Society of the Silent Walk, a seriously ill man in Amsterdam received Communion on March 15, 1345. He then vomited, and what he had brought up was thrown into a fire. The next morning, the host was said to have been found intact among the ashes. A priest took it to the parish church, but the tradition says it appeared again in the man’s house twice. These are events as handed down in a medieval devotional account, not physical observations this site can independently verify.
From chapel to procession

A chapel was later built where the event was believed to have occurred, and a procession made Amsterdam a place of pilgrimage. The annual public procession ended after the city’s 1578 change to Protestant government, when Catholic worship was restricted. The Catholic community kept the memory in more private forms, including at the Begijnhof chapel. The photograph here shows that later chapel, not the medieval site or the alleged surviving host.
The silent walk today

The Society describes a nighttime Silent Walk along the old route, without banners or spoken prayer, as a continuation of the devotion. In a 2025 lecture, the bishop of Haarlem-Amsterdam placed the 1345 story within the history of Eucharistic worship. The existence of a long-standing pilgrimage and a bishop’s commemoration establishes a living Catholic tradition; this page does not claim a modern Vatican investigation or scientific proof of the medieval event.
amsterdam.reflection: A crowded city makes room for a quiet walk. What might silence help you notice about the Eucharist and the people beside you?

ivorra.title: Ivorra: The Holy Doubt
ivorra.label: A Catalan sanctuary
ivorra.alt: Present-day Sanctuary of the Holy Doubt near Ivorra, Catalonia
ivorra.sourceLabel: Diocese of Solsona, Ivorra parish history
ivorra.source2Label: Ivorra municipal guide, Sanctuary of the Holy Doubt
ivorra.lead: A priest’s doubt during Mass is remembered in a sanctuary and a Gothic reliquary, with the earliest documents difficult to verify today.
sections: A story about doubt

The Diocese of Solsona dates the Holy Doubt of Ivorra to 1010. In the local tradition described by the Ivorra municipal guide, a priest named Bernat Oliver was celebrating Mass when he doubted the change of bread and wine. The chalice was said to overflow with blood, staining the altar cloth. The guide also recounts bells ringing on their own. These are details of a centuries-old account, not observations this site can independently verify.
Claims of early recognition

Local accounts say Bishop Ermengol of Urgell recognized the event and Pope Sergius IV confirmed it in a bull. The municipal guide reports that a papal document and stained cloth were placed under an altar and rediscovered centuries later. We have not inspected an original papal bull or an authenticated contemporary record. This page attributes the claim to the local tradition rather than presenting a surviving Vatican decree as independently verified.
A sanctuary and a reliquary

The Diocese of Solsona says a Gothic reliquary was made during a fifteenth-century revival of devotion. The municipality says a portion of stained cloth is kept at the Church of Sant Cugat, while the Sanctuary of Santa Maria near Ivorra marks the place associated with the event. Today’s sanctuary is a later building. Its continuing pilgrimage and the diocese’s account attest the local devotion, not a modern scientific ruling on the event a thousand years ago.
ivorra.reflection: The name Holy Doubt makes room for a difficult question within prayer. What helps you seek truth without turning away from reverence?

faverney.title: Faverney: The Host and the Fire
faverney.label: An episcopal inquiry
faverney.alt: Exterior of the abbey church of Notre-Dame at Faverney, France
faverney.sourceLabel: Catholic Church in France, 400th-anniversary account and interview
faverney.source2Label: Town of Faverney, chronology of the 1608 tradition
faverney.lead: After a fire in an abbey church, witnesses reported an ostensory suspended above the ashes. An archbishop's inquiry followed within weeks.
sections: A fire at Pentecost

The French bishops' conference recounts that monks exposed the Blessed Sacrament at Faverney during Pentecost in May 1608. An overnight fire consumed the display beneath an ostensory holding two consecrated hosts. When the church was opened on Monday, witnesses reported the ostensory suspended above the burned structure. Faverney's municipal account places its descent on Tuesday, during Mass, after about 33 hours. These are reported observations in a historical religious account, not a scene documented by a modern photograph.
An inquiry close to the event

The bishops' conference says the archbishop of Besançon declared the miracle authentic on July 10, 1608, after an episcopal inquiry and 54 written depositions. That is a reported historical diocesan judgment. We have not inspected the original depositions or decree, and do not turn the account into a claim of new scientific proof or a separate modern Vatican ruling.
The memory that remains

The abbey church became a place of Pentecost pilgrimage. The French bishops' conference describes a major diocesan commemoration in 2008, four centuries later, and the town records the continuing devotion to the holy hosts. The church pictured here is a present-day witness to that public memory; the photograph does not show the 1608 fire or what visitors said they saw afterward.
faverney.reflection: A community stopped to ask what had happened, then kept returning to pray. What does careful attention change in the way you approach the Eucharist?
